item.title: As Iran Truce Expires and Options Shrivel, Trump Lashes Out
item.description:
As a crumbling truce with Iran officially collapsed on Monday, President Trump signaled his frustration at his inability to resolve a war that he started but cannot seem to end.

In an interview with Fox News, the president lashed out at an American ally, Oman, that has been trying to mediate negotiations with Iran.

“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Mr. Trump said in a phone interview, according to Fox News’s Trey Yingst.

The latest threat toward Oman, which has facilitated talks between the United States and Iran for years and maintains that it is still a neutral mediator, came as Mr. Trump found himself without much leverage to reach the goals he set out at the start of the war.

“I think, ultimately, his threats against Oman are just a reflection of his frustration with the situation he’s created, where he has no good options,” said Nate Swanson, of the Atlantic Council’s Iran Strategy Project. “He’s just reflexively lashing out, and this time Oman got in the cross hairs.”

Hostilities have now stretched past the six-month mark in a conflict that began with the United States and Israel launching strikes across Iran in February. Administration officials pledged at the time that the war would be over in four to six weeks.

On the battlefield, the United States has struck thousands of targets in Iran and dealt serious blows to the country’s military capabilities, but the president has struggled to achieve the war’s political objectives.

In June, the two sides agreed to a memorandum of understanding, but that quickly fell apart. Both Mr. Trump and Iran’s leaders have said the deal is essentially dead.

“It is mostly symbolic, but symbols matter,” Justin Logan, the director of defense and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute, said of the expiration of the memorandum of understanding. He emphasized that the main function of the agreement was to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the critical shipping lane in the Persian Gulf that Iran effectively closed during the war.

“The tragic part here is that the United States is clawing to try to get back to the state of the Middle East before the war started,” he said.

As the cease-fire officially expires, the president and his team have promised to level crushing sanctions against Iran this week, though the details of those plans have yet to be unveiled. And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the United States can maintain a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz indefinitely — an acknowledgment that there was no end to the war in sight.

In the Fox News interview, Mr. Trump sought to project patience, saying he was “not in a hurry” to secure a deal while maintaining that his central goal remained preventing Iran from possessing a nuclear weapon.

Speaking to the reporters in the Oval Office, Mr. Trump was asked whether he was any closer to ending the war now than he was when the memorandum of understanding was agreed to. The president did not directly answer, but claimed that Iran wants to “make a deal, but they’re not going to make the kind of a deal that I feel is necessary.”

He added, “Look, we’re in there for one reason: Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.”

Mr. Trump also downplayed concerns that sailors on the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln have been deployed for too long with conditions worsening. The ship is supporting U.S. operations in the Middle East against Iran.

Mr. Trump called reports of food shortages on the ship “fake news.”

“The Lincoln has been out there for a period of time, good period of time, but over the years we’ve had him out there much longer,” the president said.

Mr. Trump also said the United States could declare the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States.

“We control it with the blockade, and I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” he said.

But it was Oman that received the president’s fury on Monday. Iran has said it has been holding talks with Oman on temporarily reopening the strait.

“I don’t think they behaved very well,” he said of the U.S. ally, “but we’d handle them very easily, just like we do other things.”

It was the second time this year the president has threatened the country. In May it emerged that Oman had discussed working with Iran to charge fees for ships to pass through the strait.

“Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we’ll have to blow them up,” Mr. Trump told reporters then. “They understand that. They’ll be fine.”

A White House official did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Swanson said he believed the president had several options to try to resolve the war.

He said the United States could continue with a policy of what Mr. Trump has called “low key” economic pressure, which has thus far not produced results; ramp up a military campaign against Iran, even as U.S. munition stockpiles dwindle; or return to negotiations to produce a deal similar to the one both sides already abandoned. Or, he said, Mr. Trump could wash his hands completely of the entire war, and ask Gulf allies to get more involved in the Strait of Hormuz.

“I’m wondering if at some point, either by choice or incompetence, we kind of just put our blinders on and let the Gulf figure it out,” Mr. Swanson said.

item.title: What We Know About Damages From Hurricane Lala in Hawaii
item.description:
Hawaii residents faced extensive power outages, submerged bridges and roads, and damaged homes after Hurricane Lala brushed along the islands.

Hurricane Lala, which was a Category 1 hurricane, did not make landfall but moved close enough to wash out highways, wreck properties and topple trees. Hurricanes are common in the Pacific Ocean, but landfall in Hawaii is rare because of its small size in relation to the expansive ocean. The eye of Lala did not cross over into land, but the outer bands still left significant destruction, primarily affecting people living along the southern and eastern edges of Hawaii’s Big Island.

On Sunday and Monday, residents and emergency crews continued to sift through damage. Here’s what we know:

Gov. Josh Green of Hawaii said that some areas received as much as 30 inches of rain and that there were several reported mudslides. More than 13 inches had fallen at Hilo International Airport as of Sunday night. About 35 inches of rain was recorded near Nene Cabin, a weather observation site on the southern tip of the Big Island. Laupahoehoe, on the Hamakua coastline in the northeast part of the island, measured over 43 inches during the storm, with the majority of precipitation falling within 24 hours beginning Saturday afternoon.

Hilo, on the eastern edge of the Big Island, is one of the rainiest cities in the United States, and residents are used to frequent downpours. But many residents said they were surprised at the intensity of the storm.

Hurricane Lane in 2018 similarly passed south of Hawaii and produced comparable rainfall totals in the same locations. The difference with Lala is that it came dangerously close enough to produce damaging winds, including hurricane-force winds, on the Big Island.

Residents were spared the worst of the worst, which is found in the eyewall, but the more intense side of Lala (the right side in the direction the storm is traveling) hit the Big Island directly. One wind gust at the Mauna Kea Summit measured 140 miles per hour, and another near sea level in Kona registered 78 miles per hour. (Hurricane-force winds are 74 miles per hour or greater.)

On Saturday, when the storm passed through, a 45-year-old man was killed in a head-on car accident in the southern area of the Big Island. A 21-year-old woman was critically injured from the collision.

Two paramedics were also rescued in Naaleuh, in the southern region of the Big Island, after floodwaters trapped them in their vehicle.

About 100 homes had been damaged or washed away because of the storm, Governor Green said.

Officials said that some of the worst damage may have occurred in rural places in the southern edge of the Big Island but that fallen electrical lines have complicated efforts for people to get to the area.

The coastal town of Pahala, which has about 1,800 residents, was cut off from the rest of the island after floodwaters inundated roads and bridges — six were destroyed or severely damaged, officials said. Part of a major highway also collapsed, which blocked road access to Ka’u Hospital, the region’s only hospital.

County fire officials said they were prepared to use helicopters to move patients with medical emergencies.

“There’s a lot of damage that we’ll be working on,” Governor Green said on Sunday afternoon.

More than 114,000 homes and businesses remained without power in Hawaii on Monday, down from about 200,000 customers on Sunday. That includes about 40 percent of the customers on the Big Island, which is largely rural.

Counties shown are those with at least 1 percent of customers without power. Times are Eastern. Source: PowerOutage.com The New York Times

People could face days or weeks without power because the storm downed transmission lines that connect power plants to homes and businesses. Because of widespread flooding and other challenges traveling along rural roads, officials said it could take weeks for the power to be fixed on the Big Island.

Governor Green said that schools, state and county offices and courts across the state would be closed on Monday, as Hawaii recovered from the storm and worked on restoring power. All airports and harbors reopened, according to the Hawaii Department of Transportation.

The damaged transmission lines include one that runs for 42 miles on the Big Island. In addition to knocking out power lines, the storm also damaged many of the large structures that carry the lines on the Big Island and Oahu.

Orlando Mayorquín, Amy Graff, Nazaneen Ghaffar, Ivan Penn and Jacey Fortin contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Welcome to The Local: Twin Cities
item.description:
Good afternoon, and welcome to the inaugural issue of The Local: Twin Cities. It’s a collector’s edition, suitable for framing if you happen to have a really tall and narrow frame.

You can expect us in your inbox at lunchtime on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. We’ll be sharing neighborhood news, taking you behind the scenes with Times beat reporters, talking with local notables (like Hope Walz, below) and highlighting NYT Cooking recipes with local flavor. In short: SPAM, not spam.

We’re most excited to hear from you. We want your feedback on what we’re doing, and ideas for what we should cover. And we really want your tips for enjoying the State Fair: Send them to thelocaltc@nytimes.com.

This local newsletter is an experiment, meaning there’s no rulebook. There is a style guide, however, and we’re looking into clarifying with our colleagues that “the U” is acceptable on first reference to the University of Minnesota.

We’ll tell you more about us, but first, today’s top stories:

Some Twin Cities suburbs are now more diverse than the urban centers of Minneapolis and St. Paul, Sarah Ritter at The Minnesota Star Tribune writes in this richly reported piece.

A Liberian official made a fortune operating Minnesota group homes from overseas. Listen to this MPR News investigation on how the state has struggled to regulate the industry.

Last week’s primaries set up unusually competitive and most likely historic races in November. The Pioneer Press’s Alex Derosier dives into the details of the two races and four women vying for top offices.

Sign up here to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox or share this link with a friend who might like to join us.

We’re your hosts, wearing our house shoes and relieved you arrived carrying a Bundt cake so we don’t need to figure out whether or not this is a handshake moment.

Jay was born in Minneapolis and keeps coming back, after picking up a Ph.D. in sociology at Harvard and, most recently, covering culture at the Duluth News Tribune. He’s currently settling into his new home in Northeast, enjoying the variety of cuisines and bike lanes, always on the lookout for the next must-see show.

Shadi was born in Sudan and came to the United States as a child refugee. He lived in the Twin Cities area from Head Start to high school, but then spent years away in California (Stanford), Cairo (Egypt!) and Atlanta. Eventually, the pandemic had him longing for family and familiarity, leading him back home. He loves to skydive and can’t wait to get a few jumps in soon.

Are you on WhatsApp? Join us there, too, to keep up with us between sends.

As part of this project, The New York Times will be spending more time in Minnesota. Wirecutter, The Times’s product recommendation site, will be recording a special podcast episode at the MPR booth during the fair. And we’re revealing here, for the very first time, what our experts will be reviewing on that show:

Pickles!

Of course it’s pickles. Among this year’s 36 new fair foods and drinks are pickle pie (with ranch and hot sauce frosting), a white chocolate chip cookie with chopped dills, and pickle wine.

The show will be live at noon on Sunday, Aug. 30. The Wirecutter hosts Caira Blackwell and Rosie Guerin will be joined by Maki Yazawa, writer of our guide to the best kitchen pickles, as well as Mary Bartz, the State Fair canning coordinator, and Teresa Craig, the fair’s 2025 Prestigious Processor of the Pantry.

Mark your calendar, and watch this newsletter for a guide to the State Fair pickle experience.

Gov. Tim Walz has had a tough couple of years; his approval rating dropped significantly, fueled in part by Minnesota’s fraud scandal. But his daughter, Hope Walz, nearly 1,000 miles away in Montana, has found her moment.

Hope took off on social media during her father’s vice-presidential campaign in 2024 and now has about 700,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. (Check out this interview with her from KMSP on the campaign.)

Some of Hope’s posts are political, but she also regularly does “fit checks” with her dad and has shared videos from the Lollapalooza music festival as well as appeals for donations to a homeless shelter where she works.

BringMeTheNews reported that online abuse led her to take a social media break in December. A month later, she was back on TikTok to announce, after a father-daughter midwinter run, that “Tim,” as she often calls him, would not seek a third term.

Though she lives elsewhere, Hope remains one of Minnesota’s best-known Gen Z-ers. So we picked her as our first subject for “3 Questions.” Send us your suggestions for who we should interview next.

SHADI: What is your advice for young people today?

HOPE: Lean into the little things that make you happy, even if others think it’s dumb. I’m 25, and I’m finding so much joy in the things I enjoyed when I was a kid — the color pink, watching soccer again, fun trinkets (I collect Sonny’s Angels), reality TV, reading. There is so much pressure to be “cool” nowadays, yet the coolest thing you can do is be entirely yourself.

What is your biggest fear?

Being perceived. Crazy, I know. It’s literally my job to be perceived by the world, yet I can’t think too hard about that or I’ll freak out. I find myself asking people in my real life not to look at my TikTok. It’s probably no use, but I still try.

Will you ever run for office?

My dad says, “Never turn down a job you haven’t been offered yet.” But I would still say, absolutely not. I like being able to be in my own lane and do my own thing. I think my influence runs parallel to electoral politics and there is power in that.

The Times heard from nearly 600 readers about recent revelations that the Homeland Security Department investigated left-leaning groups, sometimes using invasive tactics, during Operation Metro Surge. Lots came from our fellow Minnesotans, including some with personal experience at the protests. We’d love to hear from you, too.

As a middle-aged suburban mom who attended many local protests over the last year, I’d like to assure those who believe the protestors were all extreme leftists, or violent, or communists, or cop-haters (I’ve heard all these), that 99.9% were just ordinary folks who were fed up. The protesters were ordinary parents, grandparents, college kids, gainfully-employed mortgage-paying citizens who peacefully showed up with signs and hope for a better future. They were simply people who cared and wanted to do something, anything, to express outrage at the inhumanity and government overreach that has become too normal. That the government felt the need to infiltrate their chats, create dossiers and track their movements would be laughable if it weren’t so scary.

Not only does ICE need significant checks and balances, so too does DHS.

Given the rising risk of left-wing violence this is greatly welcomed. The idea that these are just grassroots activists is no longer true. A lot of the left in Minnesota are extremists: communists and anarchists. An unfortunate reality we now face

@Brody We engaged in peaceful nonviolent resistance to obvious unlawful tyranny. Every morning I woke up thankful that we were able to continue do so - it was incredibly hard, and an example to the entire world.

Talya Minsberg, born and raised in St. Paul, has a habit of noting every Minnesotan on any given team. She’s got today’s report:

It’s always a homecoming for Paige Bueckers, even if she’s playing against her home team.

Before Bueckers’s team, the Dallas Wings, faced the Lynx last weekend, she stopped by St. Louis Park to cut the ribbon on newly refurbished courts. The courts, where Bueckers played as a kid, are now tricked out with brightly colored designs and the star guard’s signature and handprint. It’s the second new, and beautiful, court that Bueckers has unveiled in the Twin Cities.

It’s not as if you needed a reminder that Bueckers, the No. 1 W.N.B.A. draft pick in 2025, is Minnesotan. Of course you know that she is a Hopkins High School graduate, having earned multiple national high school awards and fielding scholarship offers from the age of 14. You may have even seen Hopkins Royals jerseys dot arenas while she played for the University of Connecticut.

But you may not remember just how long sports media in the Twin Cities has been following Bueckers’s career. In 2016, Chip Scoggins, a sports columnist at The Minnesota Star Tribune, wrote about Cheryl Reeve’s chance encounter with a then-sixth-grade Bueckers. Reeve, the Lynx coach, was working out at a St. Louis Park gym and was impressed by an elementary school player shooting hoops nearby.

“She had a way about her that just oozed confidence,” Reeve said. She ran the elementary school player through drills. Read the whole, delightful piece here.

Top Times stories, selected for Minnesota readers. We have made these links free for readers of The Local.

Politics: The results of the most recent primaries in Minnesota, Michigan and Wisconsin have revealed the strength and limitations of young, progressive outsiders.

Pesticides: California is phasing out paraquat, a pesticide widely used in the U.S. and linked to Parkinson’s disease. Minnesota has considered a ban.

Needle nation: Between weight-loss drugs, peptides, I.V.F. and Botox, even needle-phobes are willing to embrace shots. Nearly one in five U.S. adults has tried an injectable GLP-1 drug like Ozempic.

Books: When is it OK to give up on a book? Everyone, it seems, has a strong opinion. “I keep hoping it will get better,” Lynn Nill, a reader from Shorewood, Minn., told The Times.

Restaurants: Times reporters, editors and photographers traveled across the U.S. in search of their favorite Mexican restaurants. Oro by Nixta made the list. “The ambitious but unpretentious restaurant is one of the reasons Northeast Minneapolis is among the country’s most alluring neighborhoods for dining,” Brett Anderson writes.

We’re off to a sunny start this week, but look out tonight and tomorrow morning for “a little bit of weather” (in technical terms, wind and rain).

Minnesotans have a lot of feelings about invasive species. Sometimes they become beloved, as in the smelt scooped out of northern waterways each spring. Sometimes they become a “lightning rod” for controversy, as MPR News reported about beautiful lupine in 2022.

MPR is back on the invasive species beat this summer, introducing us to the Buckthorn Removal Singles Club. Yes, this new group brings together people looking for love by having them clean up the East River Trail.

“For an hour and a half,” Nicole Ki reported, “they cleared invasive shrubs, piled branches and stopped every so often to introduce themselves.”

Thanks for taking a break with us this afternoon. See you Wednesday!

Hi all, we wanted to start the conversation by welcoming all of our readers! We want this newsletter to be an ongoing dialogue between us and our audience. So please let us know what you're enjoying, what you'd like to see more of, and how we can better serve the Twin Cities.

Feedback? Questions? We’d love to hear from you: thelocalTC@nytimes.com

Hosts: Shadi Bushra and Jay GablerEditor: Hanna IngberStaff Editor: Talya MinsbergIllustrations: Peter SteineckPhoto Editor: Clinton CargillStrategy: Katherine ChangEditorial Director, Newsletters: Jodi Rudoren

]]>

item.title: Mary Peltola Shakes Up Senate Campaign Staff Days Before Alaska Primary
item.description:
Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska, has shaken up her campaign in the final days before a high-profile primary, jettisoning at least one longtime senior aide and switching campaign managers. Two veteran contractors for Ms. Peltola’s campaigns were also let go.

Ms. Peltola, a former congresswoman who represents the Democratic Party’s best chance of flipping a crucial Alaska Senate seat, had enjoyed early momentum since announcing her bid in January, raising a significant amount of money and mounting a strong challenge to Senator Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican. But the days before Tuesday’s nonpartisan top-four contest have been shakier for her campaign.

She drew headlines by distancing herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris, who signed a fund-raising appeal from her PAC last week, asking donors to contribute to Ms. Peltola’s campaign. Running in a conservative state that is skeptical of national Democrats, Ms. Peltola kept Ms. Harris at arm’s length as Republicans eagerly jumped on the connection.

Last week, Ms. Peltola fired Elisa Rios, a close adviser who had helped run her two campaigns for the House and was campaign manager for her Senate bid, according to a person familiar with the move. She also fired a deputy campaign manager. The moves came before the dust-up involving Ms. Harris.

Anton McParland, another top Peltola confidant who served as her chief of staff in Congress and was running her campaign alongside Ms. Rios, “has transitioned into a new role” as a general consultant, Ms. Peltola’s campaign said.

The campaign declined to comment on the reason for the shake-up or for Mr. McParland’s new role, and also declined to make him available for comment. Ms. Peltola herself did not respond to requests for comment.

Harry Child, a spokesman for Ms. Peltola, said in a statement that “the campaign has undergone staffing updates as we transition into the general election and we appreciate the contributions of everyone who built the winning campaign to send Mary to the U.S. Senate this November.”

The campaign said that Cheryl Bruce, who had been serving as deputy campaign manager, was now Ms. Peltola’s campaign manager. And it said the contractors who were let go had been part-time workers whose services weren’t needed for the general election.

Ms. Peltola’s allies emphasized that the candidate remained in a strong position, pointing to a new poll from Data for Progress on Monday suggesting she had a lead over Mr. Sullivan.

But Republicans pounced on the news.

“Even Mary Peltola’s closest advisers know her ‘Alaska last’ campaign is a lost cause,” Nick Puglia, a spokesman for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said in a statement.

item.title: Lost a Race for Congress? Try Again in Florida.
item.description:
Ah, Florida. It’s a land of retirees, fresh starts and second acts — even, it turns out, for Republicans running for Congress.

Tuesday’s crowded primary to succeed Representative Byron Donalds, an acolyte of President Trump who is running for governor, features candidates who have run for Congress or served in Congress, all in other states.

The upshot has been a zany primary featuring candidates trying to prove their Florida bona fides and alignment with President Trump.

Carpetbaggers? Perhaps. But many Floridians hail from somewhere else. The solidly Republican 19th Congressional District, a swath of Southwest Florida’s MAGA country that stretches from Fort Myers to Marco Island, is home to many former Midwesterners. (And Trump, a New Yorker, adopted Florida as his home state.)

Two of the Republican candidates are former lawmakers attempting comebacks after their first turns in Congress ended in scandal. One is Madison Cawthorn, who lost his re-election bid in North Carolina in 2022 after a deluge of salacious accusations. The other is Chris Collins, who resigned from office in New York in 2019, as he prepared to plead guilty to insider trading charges. Trump pardoned him in December 2020, weeks before leaving office.

Then there are three candidates who have alighted on the district after losing congressional bids elsewhere. They are Catalina Lauf, who lost a Republican primary in Illinois in 2020 and a general election in the same district in 2022; Jim Oberweis, who defeated Lauf in that 2020 primary and then lost in the general election, and Ola Hawatmeh, who lost a Republican primary in New York in 2020.

Not being from Florida has not stopped candidates in the race from accusing the others of being even less from Florida.

“I’m shocked, quite frankly, that some of the other candidates have moved down here and have no experience in the area,” said Oberweis, who served two terms in the Illinois State Senate. He has owned a home in Florida for 46 years, he said, and has lived in the state full time for six.

Jim Schwartzel, a local media mogul, is also running in the primary, as are four other Republicans, for a total of 10 candidates. One of the other four, John Strand, served prison time for participating in the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack, before being pardoned by Trump.

It is Lauf, who moved to Florida after the coronavirus pandemic and has compared her family to other “blue state refugees,” who has had the momentum in the final days of the campaign. Last week, Trump endorsed her, noting that he appointed Lauf as an adviser to the Commerce Department during his first term. “She has truly been with us from the beginning!” he wrote.

In an interview, Lauf, 33, said Republican voters wanted an outsider. “A lot of these guys represent the Republican Party of the past,” she said.

To try to discredit her candidacy for being a recent Florida transplant is “pretty insulting” to voters, she added. “We’re the party of merit.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

What else we’re watching tomorrow

Remember Alex Vindman, the former national security official who was a top witness in President Trump’s first impeachment trial? He’s seeking the Democratic nomination for Senate in Florida tomorrow.

Donalds, a devoted Trump ally, is the front-runner for the Republican nomination for governor to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has not weighed in on the race.

The embattled Representative Cory Mills, a Republican, is running for re-election in Florida’s Seventh Congressional District. He has been accused of assault and is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee. He has the support of Trump — but not of all his colleagues in the House, or of DeSantis.

In Alaska, former Representative Mary Peltola is trying to make a comeback as the state’s Democratic nominee for Senate. But her campaign has been roiled by staff changes in recent days.

There’s a special election in California to replace former Representative Eric Swalwell. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee has spent heavily to oppose a progressive candidate in the race.

quote of the day

That was Katy Padilla Stout, the Texas Democrat running against the pro-gun influencer Brandon Herrera in a border district that stretches from San Antonio to El Paso.

Padilla Stout was referring to her relationship with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which recently added the district as a midterm target, saying that Herrera’s “disturbing history of extremism” had put it in play. Still, the committee has yet to send campaign funds Padilla Stout’s way.

Read more about the messy race from my colleague Bayliss Wagner.

the 10,000-foot view

A string of primary wins by progressive candidates within the Democratic Party this summer has revealed the strength of a high-energy insurgent movement — but also its possible limitations, Lisa Lerer and Katie Glueck write.

Boldly liberal candidates have shown themselves to be competitive outside deep-blue territory. But some of the voters who have historically been most crucial to the party’s fortunes remain skeptical, raising questions about whether these candidates can piece together a broad enough coalition to win general elections:

In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed trailed in majority-Black townships across the state. He also showed signs of weakness with older voters, who vote the most reliably.

In Wisconsin, the establishment-backed David Crowley had an edge in metro Milwaukee and in rural counties. The democratic socialist Francesca Hong, who lost to Crowley, showed strength in smaller cities and suburbs, as well as counties that are home to college towns.

In New York City, the democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier performed well in whiter, younger and higher-income areas, beating Representative Adriano Espaillat. But he was strong across many older and majority-Hispanic areas.

Read more here.

ONE LAST THING

President Trump won Florida by 13 percentage points in 2024. And in many Latin American communities in South Florida, socialism is a dirty word.

But three underdog democratic socialist candidates are trying to prove that the way for the Democratic Party to regain relevance in the state is by embracing the left, not by recoiling from it.

“We are not a conservative state,” Richie Floyd, a democratic socialist who is the vice chairman of the City Council in St. Petersburg, Fla., said at a recent rally. “We are not a right-wing state. We are a working-class state.”

A win for any of them would be a major upset.

Taylor Robinson and Jess Bidgood contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Trump to Travel to Myrtle Beach to Rally for Darline Graham
item.description:
President Trump is traveling to Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Friday to drum up support for Senator Darline Graham, his choice in a competitive runoff election to succeed Lindsey Graham in the Senate for a full six-year term.

The trip, announced on Monday by the South Carolina Republican Party, is the latest of many efforts by the president to put his thumb on the scale in a special primary election to replace Mr. Graham after he unexpectedly died in July.

Ms. Graham, the sister of Mr. Graham, will face Representative Ralph Norman, an ultraconservative congressman who has shown a willingness to break from the president’s agenda, in a runoff election scheduled for Aug. 25. At the urging of Mr. Trump, Ms. Graham was appointed to the seat on an interim basis by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster.

The South Carolina G.O.P. announced the visit in a statement on Friday, saying the president is “scheduled to hold a rally in Myrtle Beach on behalf of one of the runoff candidates.”

Mr. Trump has gone to great lengths to boost Ms. Graham, a longtime advocate for people with disabilities who had never held political office. He first urged her appointment to serve out the remainder of Mr. Graham’s term, making her the state’s first female senator. Then he gave Ms. Graham his coveted endorsement in the crowded primary election last week for the full six years — passing over a longtime ally in the House, Representative Russell Fry.

Ms. Graham finished in first place in the Aug. 11 special primary election, but not by enough to avoid a runoff against Mr. Norman, who finished in second. After the polls closed that day, Mr. Trump worked the phones to urge high-level officials, including Mr. Fry, to back Ms. Graham publicly.

The president will now travel to Mr. Fry’s district in Myrtle Beach, where Ms. Graham must win over the congressman’s voters to beat Mr. Norman.

It was unclear if the president’s visit indicated that the White House was concerned about Ms. Graham’s political viability. The White House did not respond to requests for information about the event on Friday.

item.title: Appeals Court Rejects Trump’s Strategy of Picking U.S. Attorneys
item.description:
A federal appeals court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s strategy of circumventing Congress to more freely appoint politically aligned federal prosecutors, casting fresh doubt on the practice.

The ruling from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco was the second appellate decision within the last year to take issue with the administration’s custom of leaving interim prosecutors in place instead of appointing permanent U.S. attorneys who require congressional confirmation.

Within hours of the ruling Monday, the Trump administration said it would appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Monday’s opinion, penned by Judge Eric D. Miller, a Trump appointee, upheld a lower court’s order disqualifying Sigal Chattah, a Trump ally who continues to lead the United States Attorney’s Office in Nevada. A series of moves by the Trump administration has kept her in office beyond the expiration of her temporary appointment. In February, a day before oral arguments before the Ninth Circuit, the administration nominated a permanent appointment, a defense lawyer named George Kelesis, but the Senate has not confirmed him.

Judge Miller, writing on behalf of a unanimous three-judge panel, ruled that the attorney general did not have the authority to “create a de facto acting U.S. attorney by delegating all of the functions and duties of the U.S. attorney to someone else.”

The Ninth Circuit decision built on another ruling, issued last December, from a three-judge panel of the Third Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that Alina Habba, a former personal lawyer for President Trump, had been serving unlawfully as the U.S. attorney in New Jersey. The Trump administration did not appeal that decision, and Ms. Habba later resigned.

Despite the earlier ruling, the practice has continued unabated. The administration has chosen to have some U.S. attorney’s offices, from Los Angeles to the Northern District of New York, run by lawyers designated as first assistants who are not subject to the congressional approval process.

While federal judges in a district can also make appointments to fill vacancies, those appointees are being immediately fired unless the judges win the administration’s approval. Last month, in a major shift, Roger Rogoff, a judicially appointed U.S. attorney in Seattle who was fired by the administration less than an hour after his appointment, filed a lawsuit contesting his termination.

James I. Pearce, a lawyer who argued against the administration before the Ninth Circuit, said in a statement that the decision “confirms what the district court — and every other court that has examined these tactics — already found: The government cannot circumvent the Senate’s role in confirming a U.S. attorney.”

Anne Joseph O’Connell, a professor at Stanford University Law School, said the Ninth Circuit ruling suggested the court was open to “a possible solution” which entailed delegating authority over the U.S. attorney’s office to more than one person. This strategy was previously rejected by a lower court judge.

The administration’s appointment practices have contributed, critics have said, to a sense of chaos within the Justice Department, which has pivoted in some instances to a retribution campaign against President Trump’s perceived enemies. The department’s record of bringing airtight cases is also withering, from its immigration-related prosecutions to the recent abandonment of a vandalism case that was related to the botched renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

item.title: Judge Rules Trump Administration Can’t Scrap F.B.I. Move to Maryland
item.description:
A federal judge in Maryland blocked the Trump administration from abandoning a planned move for the F.B.I. from its crumbling headquarters in Washington to a new facility in Prince George’s County, Md.

In a 47-page ruling, Judge Theodore Chuang of the Federal District Court in Maryland wrote that “the F.B.I. erroneously concluded” that it could select a new headquarters for itself without consulting Congress.

In reality, Judge Chuang wrote, Congress had already approved the Biden administration plan for the F.B.I. to move to Maryland. Congress had not signed off on the Trump administration’s decision to end that plan and instead move the agency to the Ronald Reagan Building in downtown Washington — a building that was recently vacated by the U.S. Agency for International Development.

“The Court therefore does not find that Congress has ratified either the Reagan Building Selection Decision or the F.B.I. Reprogramming Decision, or that it has impliedly repealed” the previous plan to move the F.B.I. headquarters to Maryland.

The ruling is almost certainly not the end of the lengthy dispute over the F.B.I.’s future headquarters. Presidents, lawmakers and agency officials have for years jockeyed over the effort to relocate the country’s premier law enforcement agency.

In the meantime, the F.B.I. continues to operate from its old headquarters, an aging colossus veiled in netting to keep concrete from falling on passers-by.

Maryland state officials cheered the ruling, which blocked the Trump administration from diverting about $1 billion to be spent on a sprawling campus near the Greenbelt Metro station in Prince George’s County.

“This case is about more than a building,” said Anthony G. Brown, the Maryland state attorney general. “It’s about ensuring that when Congress makes a decision, the Trump administration does not get to ignore it because they do not like the outcome.”

The F.B.I. did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but Mr. Trump has long opposed the move to Maryland. Since the start of his second term, he has made it clear that he would ignore the 2023 pact negotiated by the Biden administration that would relocate the bureau to Greenbelt.

“They were going to build an F.B.I. headquarters three hours away in Maryland, a liberal state,” Mr. Trump said last year, exaggerating the time needed to commute to a Washington suburb with access to the city’s Metro train system.

“We’re going to stop it,” he added.

Mr. Trump had previously sought to block the bureau from moving out of the city.

In 2018, he discarded plans to select a site in Virginia or Maryland.

item.title: Facing Quagmire in Iran, Trump Turns to a Familiar Face: North Korea’s Kim Jong-un
item.description:
The last time President Trump vowed to halt a country’s nuclear weapons program, he held three face-to-face meetings with Kim Jong-un of North Korea, declared that the two men had developed a “great relationship” and walked away empty-handed.

That was in Mr. Trump’s first term. Not only did the diplomatic effort fail, but Mr. Kim immediately hit the accelerator on his program and today possesses roughly 60 nuclear weapons, by some estimates, as well as missiles that appear capable of reaching the United States — exactly the combination Mr. Trump had vowed to dismantle.

For months now, proliferation experts have questioned whether Mr. Trump could also end up walking away from his efforts to check Iran’s nuclear program — especially now that he appears to be more focused on getting the Strait of Hormuz open than on dealing with Iran’s stockpiles of uranium, which are buried under rubble after the United States bombed them in June 2025.

Stymied in Iran, Mr. Trump is increasingly turning his sights back to North Korea, even though analysts see little hope of quickly dismantling that country’s growing nuclear arsenal.

Mr. Trump’s social media declaration on Sunday night, praising Mr. Kim and publicly ordering Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to diminish America’s role in an annual military exercise with South Korea, one of America’s allies in the Pacific, appeared intended to signal that he wants to resume negotiations. A day later, it remained unclear just how the Pentagon would scale back its role in the 11-day exercise, and a one-line statement sent to reporters by the Pentagon press office on Monday afternoon did not provide any clarity.

“The Department of War is actively working on executing the commander in chief’s directive,” the statement said, using the Trump administration’s name for the Department of Defense.

Robert Litwak, a scholar at George Washington University who has written about the nuclear programs in both North Korea and Iran, called the contrast between Mr. Trump’s approaches to those two countries “an incredible tale of two rogue states.”

“We’re at war with Iran, a nuclear-threshold state,” he said. “But with North Korea we are placating a dictator who can target the U.S. homeland with nuclear weapons.”

Mr. Trump’s outburst was also aimed at punishing the South Koreans for declining to join in the war against Iran, a position that deeply angered Mr. Trump. It was a point he made in the same social media post and reiterated to reporters in the Oval Office on Monday.

The president has also been angry that Seoul has been slow to deliver on what the White House believes is a $350 billion promise for new investments, including in shipbuilding. Last October, Mr. Trump visited South Korea and celebrated its future investments in the United States, including a promised multibillion-dollar expansion of Samsung’s chip-making plant in Texas.

“Trump defaults back to the complaint about South Korean free-riding” on America’s troop presence on the Korean Peninsula, said Scott A. Snyder, the president and chief executive of the Korea Economic Institute of America, “and he uses the security relationship as a lever to put more pressure on the South Korean government.”

Looming over the tensions is Mr. Trump’s inability to extract the United States from the Iran war. He has hinted at his eagerness in recent months to move on from that conflict and return to dealing with Mr. Kim — who indulged Mr. Trump’s desire for leader-to-leader talks with those summits during Mr. Trump’s first term.

President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea said in June that Mr. Trump appeared to want to resume talks with Mr. Kim, and Mr. Trump posted a picture of himself with the North Korean leader on social media at least twice in recent months.

“Kim Jong Un and I get along GREAT!” Mr. Trump wrote alongside a photograph he posted on Saturday of their meeting at the border between North and South Korea in 2019.

Mr. Trump followed that up with another chummy post on Monday, this one a meme showing Mr. Kim making a phone call with military officers standing behind him. The caption read: “Hey Donald, we cool … right?”

The North Korean nuclear program has been a deep concern since the late 1980s, long before Iran’s nuclear program was on the radar. In 1994, during a crisis triggered by North Korea’s expulsion of international nuclear inspectors, the Clinton administration debated a military strike on the North Korean facility at Yongbyon. But it held back, and later that year former President Jimmy Carter struck a deal with Kim Il-sung, the grandfather of the current North Korean leader, to end the nuclear program in return for help building civilian nuclear reactors.

It all fell apart, and subsequent efforts to bring the North Korean program under control failed. In 2006, the North conducted its first nuclear test, and followed with five more, the most recent in 2017.

The next year, having labeled Mr. Kim “Little Rocket Man,” Mr. Trump met the North Korean leader in Singapore. After their encounter, he told a New York Times reporter that he expected that the North would dismantle its program fast. “It’s going to go very quickly,” he said after the summit. “I really believe that it’s going to go fast. And it is a very substantial arsenal. There’s no question about it.”

But while Mr. Trump recalls the encounters fondly — during the first term, he would bring out Mr. Kim’s letters to him and read excerpts to visitors in the Oval Office — they went down in history as a diplomatic failure. A second summit, in Vietnam, ended with a collapse of the talks. Mr. Trump went into the sessions ill-prepared, his national security adviser at the time, John R. Bolton, said later, and the effort fell apart when Mr. Kim refused to dismantle facilities outside the main enrichment and reprocessing center at Yongbyon.

Some fear the same thing could happen again. “Another Trump-Kim summit, which is what the president seems to be angling for, could be a disaster,” said Joel S. Wit, a former State Department diplomat who was involved in early talks with the North and wrote a history of the effort, “Fallout: The Inside Story of America’s Failure to Disarm North Korea.”

“Trump doesn’t seem to realize that the Kim Jong-un of today isn’t interested in better relations with the United States,” Mr. Wit said. “He is hellbent on keeping his nuclear weapons, sending troops to Ukraine to support his Russian ally and threatening South Korea.”

On Monday, critics of Mr. Trump’s foreign policy quickly attacked the president for undercutting a key alliance. Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said Mr. Trump had made “another inane, haphazard decision” that punished South Korea “for no reason beyond Trump’s ego.”

Victor D. Cha, a Georgetown University professor who worked on Asia policy in the George W. Bush White House, described Mr. Trump’s social media outburst as a symptom, at least in part, of the president’s frustration over Iran. He noted that Mr. Trump’s charm offensive directed at Mr. Kim came as the president tried to maintain his hard line against Tehran, a study in contrasts in Mr. Trump’s approach to perhaps the world’s two most vexing nuclear proliferation challenges.

“He’s kind of trending in two opposite directions,” Mr. Cha said. “He’s trending in the direction of pragmatically negotiating with a nuclear North Korea. But in the case of Iran, he’s taken an absolutist stance.”

Mr. Trump defended his approach to North Korea in the Oval Office on Monday. Asked by a reporter whether he was prioritizing the interests of U.S. adversaries over allies, the president shot back: “I’m making it much safer.”

“Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” the president added. “I understand him. He understands me.”

But Mr. Kim is also closely watching Mr. Trump’s war on Iran, analysts say. That war has shown North Korea, Mr. Cha said, “that they are right to pursue nuclear weapons to avoid a military strike.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Trump Votes by Mail Again in Florida
item.description:
President Trump voted by mail ahead of Florida’s Republican primary on Tuesday, according to the White House, participating for at least the third time in a practice that he has railed against for years and has equated to cheating.

Mr. Trump voted by mail in Palm Beach County in 2020, and did so again earlier this year in the special election between Democrat Emily Gregory and Republican Jon Maples to represent the district in the Florida statehouse. Records show Mr. Trump has been registered to vote there since 2019.

Politico earlier reported that Mr. Trump had voted by mail in Tuesday’s primary, citing voting records from Palm Beach Country, home to Mar-a-Lago, his private club. The New York Times could not access these records through the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections website, which said that Mr. Trump’s voting record was “protected from public disclosure.”

In an unsigned statement, the Palm Beach elections office confirmed that it had blocked access to Mr. Trump’s voting records, saying that the publicly available documents were “intended for use by a registered voter to determine his or her voter registration and voting status. Voters with protected information will not appear in this search.”

Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, confirmed that Mr. Trump voted by mail in the primary, saying that “this is a non-story.”

“As everyone knows, the President is a resident of Palm Beach and participates in Florida elections, but he obviously primarily lives at the White House in Washington, D.C.,” she said, repeating a White House statement about Mr. Trump’s last vote by mail, in March.

Mr. Trump has continued to push, for Republicans in Congress to pass legislation ahead of the midterms that would strengthen voter identification requirements and make mail-in voting significantly more difficult. There was not enough Republican support to push through the legislation this year, and senators abandoned the effort so they could get home to their states to campaign for re-election.

Mr. Trump has long fixated on mail-in-voting to bolster his baseless claims of widespread voter fraud, and has called the SAVE Act one of the most consequential pieces of legislation in the country’s history. During his State of the Union address, Mr. Trump falsely claimed that “cheating is rampant in our elections” and called for “no more crooked mail-in ballots,” though states that vote entirely by mail see little fraud.

item.title: House Panel Investigates Charges a Democrat Had Sexual Contact With Aide
item.description:
The House Ethics Committee announced on Monday that it was investigating whether Representative Jimmy Gomez had engaged in inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer, as the California Democrat conceded he had made “personal mistakes” outside his marriage.

Mr. Gomez, 51, who represents parts of Los Angeles, said in a statement that he regretted his mistakes, but he denied any wrongdoing, saying that his actions “were consensual in nature and haven’t violated the law or House Ethics rules.”

“That doesn’t diminish the impact that these mistakes have made on those I care about the most,” Mr. Gomez said. “I take full responsibility and have committed myself to working through the pain privately with my wife and family.”

House rules instituted in 2018, after the #MeToo movement focused attention on sexual misconduct in the workplace, forbid members from engaging in sexual conduct with their own aides or those working on committees on which they serve. But the rules do not bar lawmakers from having relationships with other staff members whom they do not supervise.

In the statement announcing the investigation, Representative Michael Guest of Mississippi, the Republican chairman of the Ethics Committee, and Representative Mark DeSaulnier of California, its top Democrat, cited a clause of the rules that prohibits members from “unwelcome sexual advances or conduct” toward other lawmakers or House employees.

The inquiry into Mr. Gomez’s conduct comes months after the resignations of two lawmakers facing sexual misconduct accusations — Representatives Eric Swalwell, Democrat of California, and Tony Gonzales, Republican of Texas — forced the House to confront its handling of such complaints.

Mr. Gomez, who joined Congress in 2017, had been the chairman of Mr. Swalwell’s campaign for governor but withdrew from the position after Mr. Swalwell was accused of sexually assaulting a former staff member and of sexual misconduct with other women, charges he denies.

The Ethics Committee did not provide details on what prompted its investigation, and noted in its statement that the mere fact of the inquiry did not indicate that any wrongdoing had been found. But The New York Post reported in April that Mr. Gomez had kissed a member of another office’s congressional staff in 2023. CNN reported in June that the committee was investigating Mr. Gomez, who is running for re-election against another Democrat.

The committee, a bipartisan panel responsible for policing members’ behavior, has been under pressure from several lawmakers and outside groups who complain that it is too slow to investigate claims of misconduct.

Earlier this month, Representative Chuck Edwards, Republican of North Carolina, ended his re-election campaign after the panel said that it had “substantial reason to believe” that he “violated House rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.” That investigation took fewer than four months, according to the committee's report.

House leaders have tasked Representatives Kat Cammack, Republican of Florida, and Teresa Leger Fernández, Democrat of New Mexico, to propose changes to how the Ethics Committee handles such allegations.

Several lawmakers have proposed that the House change its code of conduct to prohibit members of Congress from having sexual relationships with any staff member.

item.title: Family Presses for Information About Fatal ICE Shooting in Maine
item.description:
The Department of Homeland Security said its inspector general would investigate the fatal shooting of a Colombian immigrant by an agent last month in Maine, but scant information about the effort has frustrated the victim’s family.

The man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, was killed by an immigration agent during a July 13 confrontation in the coastal city of Biddeford. Neither the D.H.S. nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement has said publicly whether Mr. Durán Guerrero, 25, was the target of the enforcement operation. But the D.H.S. defended the officer who opened fire, saying he had done so while “fearing for public safety.”

In an effort to draw attention to the many unanswered questions, Democratic members of Congress held a public forum on Monday in Biddeford and were joined by Mr. Durán Guerrero’s relatives in demanding more information.

The auditorium where the forum was held was packed, with about 200 people, many of them wearing T-shirts and carrying placards critical of ICE. The crowd punctuated the lawmakers’ comments with raucous applause, and occasional chants of “ICE out,” and “abolish ICE.”

Representative Chellie Pingree, a Democrat of Maine, who organized the forum, said that the lack of video footage was concerning.

“If there were active body cameras on every law enforcement member who was participating there, we wouldn’t be looking at some scratchy videos from one store that’s over here, or one person that’s standing in their doorway that’s trying to get it,” Ms. Pingree said at a news conference after the hearing. “We would actually know every moment that’s happened at the scene.”

The shooting in Maine came less than a week after a fatal immigration encounter in Houston, and the two deaths prompted a fresh wave of attention on aggressive enforcement tactics by federal agents carrying out President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

Ben Gideon, a lawyer representing the family of Mr. Durán Guerrero, said at the news conference that the man’s partner, Karolina Rojas, has been interviewed by state investigators but had not been contacted by any of the federal agencies involved.

“Any reasonable investigation would include interviewing the family and eyewitnesses,” Mr. Gideon said.

The D.H.S. had said that agents were monitoring what they believed to be the home of someone who was in the country illegally and had been issued a removal order.

The D.H.S. and the Department of Justice declined to answer direct questions about whether the killing was being investigated. The Justice Department referred the question to the D.H.S., which said that its inspector general would investigate the discharge of the agent’s firearm but said nothing about investigating Mr. Durán Guerrero’s death.

Immigration agents have shot at more than 20 people during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, including many who were in vehicles, some of them fatally.

Mr. Durán Guerrero had a pending asylum application and a valid work permit, and no removal order, Ms. Pingree said.

Mr. Durán Guerrero had worked as a food delivery driver and a cleaner at a veterinary clinic. He and his partner had a 3-year-old daughter.

Gov. Janet Mills of Maine said at the hearing that she was heartbroken by the shooting but that she was confident that the state attorney general, Aaron Frey, will conduct a thorough investigation.

Mayor Liam LaFountain of Biddeford also addressed the officials. He said that Biddeford has been devastated by the shooting and that there has been no federal support to deal with the aftermath.

“The authority was federal,” Mr. LaFountain said. “The burden has been local.”

Omar Durán, Mr. Durán Guerrero’s father, said he feels “a deep pain” when Mr. Durán Guerrero’s daughter asks why her father doesn’t come home from work.

“The death of Johan Sebastián, under those conditions, at the hands of ICE, fills our community with fear and uncertainty,” he said. “That is why I ask only of God and of the justice system that my son’s case be brought to light, along with the case of the many others who have had to go through something like this.”

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: U.S. Airman Says He Would Accept Punishment for Protesting Iran War
item.description:
Maj. Jason Watson, a U.S. airman arrested after calling for President Trump’s removal over the Iran War, said on Monday that he was willing to accept punishment for his dissent.

An active-duty officer can be punished for “disloyal statements” or “contemptuous words” against the commander in chief and high-ranking government officials, an offense that can lead to dishonorable discharge, forfeiture of pay and a monthslong prison sentence.

“If I don’t put myself out there in a big way, then it’s just noise,” Major Watson said on Monday in an interview on CNN. “What is the highest price that I am willing to pay? And this is what I ultimately came up with.”

During the interview, Major Watson characterized the war in Iran as an act of American aggression and compared the U.S. military actions to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. He said the president “chose” the war despite consternation and advice against it within his cabinet officials, calling it “unconstitutional.” Major Watson added that his public dissent was motivated by his “oath to the Constitution” and urged other Americans to do the same.

“You do not have to be somebody special to take action and reject this government,” he said on CNN.

The Department of Defense referred questions to the Air Force, which did not immediately respond.

In July, Major Watson was arrested at the U.S. Capitol after attending a news conference organized by the Removal Coalition, an activist group that has called for Mr. Trump’s impeachment, conviction and removal from office.

After the news conference that Representative Al Green, Democrat of Texas, also attended, the major stood on the Capitol steps holding signs calling for the president’s removal. The U.S. Capitol Police then arrested him for unlawfully protesting on the steps of the House.

The D.C. attorney general’s office decided not to prosecute Major Watson, but he was later taken into custody by the Air Force. Soon after his arrest, Troy E. Meink, the Air Force secretary, said on social media that his office would open an investigation into Major Watson’s conduct because it “takes allegations of misconduct seriously” including “any that might undermine the nonpartisan nature” of the military.

Mr. Watson said that he was not a member of the Democratic Party.

Military law, specifically Article 88 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, mandates punishment against “any commissioned officer who uses contemptuous words” against the president, the vice president, Congress, civilian military leaders, any governor or state legislature. Article 134 punishes statements “made with the intent to promote disloyalty or disaffection toward the United States” by members of the military.

item.title: Hegseth Campaigns for Vulnerable House Republican in Iowa
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth campaigned on Monday in Iowa for Representative Zach Nunn, stepping into the political arena in a way previous leaders of the Pentagon have avoided.

Mr. Hegseth appeared at a veteran-focused fund-raising event at the Iowa State Fair alongside Mr. Nunn, who is one of the most vulnerable House Republicans in this year's midterms. He touted Mr. Nunn’s candidacy and was sharply critical of previous Democratic administrations.

“We’re restoring the warrior ethos inside our department because that matters,” Mr. Hegseth said. “We need guys like this man right here having our back in Congress.”

Mr. Hegseth also remarked on his presence at the event. “According to the lawyers, I’m only here in a personal capacity today, as a veteran and a patriotic American,” he said.

“I have to say that,” he added.

Asked about his participation in the event, the Pentagon also said Mr. Hegseth was attending in his personal capacity.

The appearance was another departure from previous norms for Mr. Hegseth, who in May campaigned in Kentucky for Ed Gallrein. Mr. Gallrein went on to defeat Representative Thomas Massie, one of Mr. Trump’s most outspoken Republican critics. In past administrations, Pentagon officials generally kept a distance from campaign activities.

Speaking to an enthusiastic crowd at a bar on the fairgrounds, Mr. Hegseth praised Mr. Nunn, an Air Force Reserve colonel, as a key supporter of the military. Mr. Nunn, who is seeking a third term, served the Air Force for nearly two decades.

“When we need an ally to call who understands why it’s important to fund our military in the way we need to fund it, but also do so in a fiscally responsible way, we call Congressman Zach Nunn,” Mr. Hegseth said.

Mr. Nunn is facing Sarah Trone Garriott, who is a Democratic state senator and a Lutheran minister, in November. Democrats are looking to win back the House majority in November; and Mr. Nunn’s seat is seen as an important battleground in the fight for control of the chamber.

The visit by Mr. Hegseth to Iowa, which has long been a key early state in the Republican presidential nominating process, could also fuel speculation about his future political plans.

In his remarks, Mr. Hegseth made jabs at former Presidents Joseph R. Biden and Barack Obama, saying his department is now prioritizing “deterrence” capabilities. He also used a derogatory term for transgender people, apparently referring to the Biden administration’s reversal of a ban on transgender service members from Mr. Trump’s first term. Mr. Trump revoked that order in January 2025.

Mr. Hegseth’s partisan message and combative style diverged from that of the candidate he was supporting. Just before Mr. Nunn’s supporters crowded into JR’s Southpork Ranch, the bar where the event was held, Mr. Nunn stood up on the fair’s famed soapbox and touted his work with both parties.

“We’ve been able to pass three bills and get them signed into law under Joe Biden, and I don’t always agree with Joe Biden very much,” Mr. Nunn said of his legislative team. “But we also had 27 bills signed into law under President Trump.”

Also present at Monday’s event were Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks, another vulnerable Republican, and Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for a competitive, open Senate seat against Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative.

item.title: A California County Eyes a New Hire: Tina Peters, the Election Denier
item.description:
Two months after her early release from prison, the election denier Tina Peters has a new job prospect: helping to oversee voting in a conservative corner of Northern California where claims of election fraud have taken root.

The news came on Sunday, when Clint Curtis, the clerk and registrar of voters in Shasta County, Calif., told a conservative radio host that he was planning to bring Ms. Peters on board next month as the new assistant registrar of voters.

“She has experience,” Mr. Curtis said. “And she’s able to take the rocks and arrows.”

Ms. Peters, who was a Colorado county clerk, was convicted in 2024 for tampering with voting machines in a scheme to show that the 2020 election was rigged against President Trump.

It was unclear how real Mr. Curtis’s job offer actually was or whether Ms. Peters would accept it. Ms. Peters’s prison sentence was commuted, but the terms of her parole limit her ability to leave Colorado. And Mr. Curtis will only be in office until January, after losing the June election to a former elections official whom he had fired.

Mr. Curtis’s announcement immediately divided people in the county, where voters alienated by the liberal areas farther south periodically vow to break away to form their own “State of Jefferson.”

Some Trump faithful in Shasta cheered the potential arrival of Ms. Peters, one of the most famous figures in the election denial movement. Moderates and traditional Republicans bemoaned the ridicule and scrutiny that would come if their elections were handed over to Ms. Peters.

“It would continue to stoke controversy, divisiveness and increase distrust in our elections,” said Matt Plummer, a Republican member of the county’s officially nonpartisan board of supervisors.

Mr. Plummer said he had been deluged by emails over the past day from residents saying they did not want Ms. Peters running their elections.

Senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat, also weighed in on social media, to say that Ms. Peters’s hiring “should be stopped immediately.” The office of Gov. Gavin Newsom said that the state was investigating reports of Ms. Peters’s potential hiring.

Peter Ticktin, a lawyer for Ms. Peters, said she was considering an offer from Shasta County, but “there’s no decision made at this point.”

Ms. Peters was released from prison in June after Gov. Jared Polis of Colorado commuted her nine-year prison sentence, but the terms of her parole require her to find employment and forbid her to leave the state or change her Colorado residence without her parole officer’s permission.

A spokeswoman for Colorado’s Department of Corrections did not immediately respond to questions about whether Ms. Peters had sought permission to travel to Shasta County.

Ms. Peters has traveled out of state since her release, including a trip to the White House where she met with Mr. Trump, one of her staunchest allies, who spent months browbeating Colorado to release her. Last week, a court hearing uncovered evidence that Trump administration officials had organized a “brainstorm call” on how to cut federal funding for Colorado as the president publicly seethed over its mail-in voting practices and the conviction of Ms. Peters.

Mr. Curtis, an election skeptic from Florida, was appointed last April to serve as Shasta County’s clerk and registrar of voters, and his tenure has been marked by conflict.

Former elections officials said there have been spelling errors on ballots and filing mistakes during his tenure. Last week, the county’s conservative board of supervisors censured him, though he denied any misconduct, according to news media reports.

Some county officials were skeptical when Mr. Curtis told a conservative radio host on KCNR that he was going to “pull in” Ms. Peters as the county’s new assistant registrar.

Shasta County officials said that position was already occupied and that there had been no formal proposal to replace that employee. Mr. Curtis told The Atlantic he would be hiring Ms. Peters as a consultant, a move that county officials said could give him more leeway.

Mr. Curtis did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment on Monday.

Ms. Peters would also have to undergo a criminal history check, according to the county’s hiring policies, although county officials said it was unclear whether her felony convictions would automatically disqualify her.

“It’s hard to know how real any of it is,” said Mr. Plummer, the county supervisor. “There are a lot of things said by our current registrar of voters..”

California is suing the county over a ballot measure approved by local voters that would ban most mail-in voting, require hand counts of ballots and mandate that voters present government-issued photo identification.

The office of the clerk and registrar of voters has been roiled by turnover over the past two years, as well as the turmoil of Mr. Curtis’s 15-month-long tenure.

Cathy Darling Allen, a Democrat who served as Shasta’s clerk and registrar of voters from 2004 to her retirement in 2024, said its elections had enough problems without Ms. Peters.

“Is this of any benefit to anyone in Shasta County?” she asked. “It’s just more chaos, more drama.”

Laurel Rosenhall contributed reporting.
